newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav 1997 economic policy seen too ambitious.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav 1997 economic policy seen too ambitious.

text.p: The Yugoslav government's 1997 economic policy plans are overly ambitious, a long way from reality and the growth projections are impossible to achieve, economists said.
The 1997 economic policy assumes 13 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) and a 48 percent surge in exports.
It also relies heavily on hopes that Yugoslavia will soon restore ties with the international financial community and the World Trade Organisation.
At a two-day economic forum of top Yugoslav economists the policy was criticised for failing to explain how these growth rates would be achieved.

"The government follows its economically unfounded projections, and the public thinks economists are behind those projections," Mladjen Kovacevic, professor at the Belgrade School of Economics told the forum.
"It is high time we became more serious and confessed to the public that our economy is in huge difficulties," he said.

Stojan Stamenkovic of the Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) said Yugoslavia faced complete uncertainty. There were big political problems surrounding future Yugoslav ties with the world community and the status of its foreign debt.

IEN called for genuine restructuring of the economy, rehabilitation of the insolvent banking sector, fast and compulsory privatisation, a flexible dinar exchange rate and the introduction of real strict budgetary limits.
Stamenkovic said Yugoslavia needed at least $2 billion a year in foreign investment to keep the economy alive and to pay some $600 million in interest rates on its foreign debt.
Tomislav Popovic, head of the IEN, said Yugoslavia like many other countries proved that inflation can be curbed, but long term stability depended on structural reforms.

Popovic qualified the government's policy as an optimistic scenario full of theoretical hypotheses, including too many "ifs" regarding bank rehabilitation and a return to the international financial community.
"There are too many assumptions for such an explosive economic growth," Popovic said.
IEN has given three scenarios, but the moderate one assumes 3-4 percent GDP growth, and only if foreign investment comes.
Economists said the government needed to address the issue of 6.6 billion marks in frozen hard currency savings on private accounts.
"The government should consider swapping this debt for shares of the most profitable companies, instead of offering a stake in insolvent Yugoslav banks," another economist Dejan Soskic said.

Referring to the government's claims that there is no budget deficit, Soskic cautioned that Yugoslavia had a hidden fiscal deficit in the form of huge losses of state companies and big amounts in overdue but unpaid pensions and wages.

And he said it may not be wise for Yugoslavia to use bonds to cover its state deficits. "It only means delaying liabilities. Instead, the government should review all aspects of public spending and reduce them, he said.
Zoran Popov of the Economics Institute said it was unlikely Yugoslavia will strike a deal with the IMF and World Bank during first half 1997, and maybe not until year-end.
"Therefore it is not realistic to expect substantial inflow of foreign capital during 1997," Popov told Reuters.
He said there will be no radical and swift market reforms, privatisation or restructuring. "Reforms will continue, but very slowly." -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
